In this paper, we propose Generative Markov Networks (GMNs), a novel class of generative models capable of discovering this latent order from unordered datasets. GMNs combine the strengths of Markov chains and generative modeling to learn both the transition probabilities between samples and the distribution of the samples themselves. We introduce a training objective based on the maximum likelihood estimation of the latent sequence, allowing the model to recover the inherent ordering of the data. We evaluate our approach on several synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating that GMNs can effectively recover the underlying order and provide superior generative performance compared to baseline models.

Unlike traditional methods that rely on manual tagging or keyword matching, our approach, Prob2Vec, learns a continuous vector representation of mathematical problems by analyzing their structural and semantic components. We treat mathematical expressions and problem descriptions as sequences of tokens, employing a skip-gram architecture to capture the latent relationships between problems. We evaluate Prob2Vec on a large-scale dataset of mathematics problems, demonstrating that it significantly outperforms baseline retrieval methods in terms of semantic similarity and pedagogical relevance. Our results indicate that Prob2Vec can effectively facilitate the discovery of analogous problems, thereby improving the efficiency of adaptive tutoring systems.

In particular, recurrent meta-learning leverages the ability of recurrent neural networks to learn an optimization procedure that can quickly adapt to new tasks. However, training these models often involves significant computational overhead and instability due to the challenges of backpropagating through long sequences of task-specific updates. To address these issues, we introduce NORML (Nodal Optimization for Recurrent Meta-Learning), a framework that employs a nodal optimization strategy to refine the learning process. By optimizing parameters at a nodal level within the recurrent structure, NORML reduces the variance of the meta-gradients and accelerates convergence. We evaluate our approach on several few-shot learning benchmarks, demonstrating that NORML achieves superior performance and faster adaptation compared to existing state-of-the-art meta-learning methods.

However, the irregular structure of sparse kernels often leads to inefficient memory access and limited hardware acceleration on actual mobile devices. To address this challenge, we propose a novel structured sparsity framework that optimizes the kernel layout for better hardware compatibility. By employing a hardware-aware pruning strategy and a specialized inference engine, we significantly reduce the computational latency and memory footprint. Our experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a substantial reduction in parameters and FLOPs while maintaining accuracy comparable to dense models, providing a practical path toward deploying high-performance CNNs on resource-constrained edge devices.

However, the computational complexity of training these models becomes prohibitive as the size of the training set grows. To address this challenge, we propose a method for constructing small coresets—weighted subsets of the original data—that provide a provable approximation of the optimal SVM solution. Our approach utilizes a sensitivity-based sampling strategy to select a small number of representative points that maintain the margin and the decision boundary of the full dataset. We provide theoretical guarantees on the coreset size and the approximation error, demonstrating that the number of points required is independent of the total number of training examples. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets show that our method significantly reduces training time and memory requirements while maintaining classification accuracy comparable to that of the full dataset.

The proposed framework, UaiNets, leverages a small amount of labeled data to iteratively refine the decision boundary of a pre-trained unsupervised model. We introduce an active learning strategy that selects the most informative samples for labeling by balancing uncertainty and diversity, thereby maximizing the gain in detection performance per labeled instance. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate that UaiNets significantly outperforms purely unsupervised methods and achieves competitive results compared to supervised approaches, while requiring far fewer labeled examples.

We propose a baseline-corrected space-by-time non-negative matrix factorization (BC-STNMF) method to decompose the population activity into a set of spatial and temporal components. By incorporating a baseline correction term, our method can effectively separate the stimulus-evoked activity from the spontaneous background activity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of BC-STNMF on a dataset of recorded spike trains from the primary visual cortex of macaques. Our results show that BC-STNMF can recover the underlying stimulus-evoked patterns and improve the decoding accuracy of the stimulus compared to standard NMF and other baseline-correction methods.

We show that deep neural networks with circulant matrices can approximate any continuous function on a compact set to any given accuracy, provided the network is sufficiently deep. Our results provide a theoretical justification for the use of circulant matrices in deep learning and suggest that the parameter reduction achieved by using circulant matrices does not necessarily come at the cost of expressive power.

In this paper, we propose ModifAE, a novel image transformation framework that eliminates the need for adversarial training. By utilizing a modified autoencoder to learn a latent space that can be manipulated via a learned transformation vector, ModifAE enables efficient and stable image-to-image translation. We show that our approach significantly reduces training time and avoids the instability typically associated with GANs, while maintaining high image quality. We evaluate ModifAE on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating its ability to generalize to unseen images and its competitiveness with state-of-the-art adversarial methods.

In the MCFS setting, the large number of classes often leads to increased inter-class similarity and a higher risk of overfitting. To address these challenges, we propose MahiNet, a neural network that leverages class hierarchy to facilitate knowledge transfer across related categories. By incorporating hierarchical constraints into the embedding space, MahiNet allows the model to share representations among classes within the same branch of the hierarchy, effectively augmenting the available information for few-shot classes. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate that MahiNet significantly outperforms existing few-shot learning baselines in both supervised and meta-learning settings.

To address these issues, we propose the Deli-Fisher GAN, which leverages a structured latent generative space informed by the Fisher Information Matrix. By incorporating the Fisher information to regularize the generator's latent space, we ensure a more stable training trajectory and improve the efficiency of the sampling process. Our method effectively constrains the latent space to better reflect the underlying data manifold, leading to higher-quality image synthesis and reduced training time. We evaluate our approach on multiple benchmark datasets, demonstrating that the Deli-Fisher GAN achieves superior performance in terms of image fidelity and stability compared to existing state-of-the-art GANs.

To address this, we propose an adversarial learning framework that encourages the shared representation to be task-invariant. By employing a task discriminator and a gradient reversal layer, we force the encoder to learn features that are useful for all tasks but do not contain task-specific information that could lead to negative transfer. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate that it consistently outperforms standard multi-task learning approaches, effectively mitigating negative transfer and improving overall performance.

These attacks often exploit the overconfidence of the model, where small perturbations in the input lead to large shifts in the logit space. In this paper, we propose a method to calibrate the logit vectors of neural networks to improve their robustness against such adversarial perturbations. By adjusting the scale and distribution of the logits, we reduce the network's sensitivity to small input changes and mitigate the impact of adversarial noise. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, showing that calibrated networks are more resilient to common adversarial attacks, such as the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), while maintaining high accuracy on clean data.

However, these methods often struggle to balance exploration and exploitation, particularly in high-dimensional landscapes where they are prone to converging to local optima. In this paper, we propose SHE2, a novel framework that leverages stochastic Hamiltonian dynamics to enhance the search process within the trust region. By introducing a momentum-based exploration mechanism governed by a stochastic differential equation, SHE2 can effectively escape local minima and explore the parameter space more efficiently than traditional random-sampling approaches. We evaluate SHE2 on a range of challenging benchmark functions and real-world machine learning problems, demonstrating that it achieves superior convergence rates and finds higher-quality solutions compared to existing derivative-free trust region methods.

However, they are often treated as black boxes, and it is difficult to understand how their internal representations relate to the semantic properties of the data they generate. In this paper, we propose a method to uncover the modularity of these models by using counterfactuals. We show that by intervening on the latent space, we can identify specific dimensions or directions that correspond to semantic attributes, such as pose or color in images. We demonstrate our approach on several datasets and show that it can be used to discover and manipulate these attributes without requiring labeled data. Our results suggest that generative models naturally learn a modular representation of the data, and that counterfactual interventions provide a powerful way to explore and understand this structure.

However, most of these methods treat the problem as a black-box mapping from low-resolution (LR) to high-resolution (HR) images, neglecting the underlying physical degradation process. In this paper, we propose a framework that treats CNNs as inverse problem solvers to better model the image formation process. We introduce a Double Network (DN) architecture, which consists of a degradation network that learns the forward mapping from HR to LR and a restoration network that learns to invert this process. By jointly optimizing these two networks, we can effectively incorporate the degradation prior into the SR task. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art SR methods in terms of both PSNR and visual quality.

Traditional synthesis methods rely on hand-crafted models, while deep learning approaches often struggle to produce high-quality audio. In this paper, we propose SynthNet, a framework for learning synthesizers end-to-end. SynthNet consists of a differentiable synthesizer that can be optimized using gradient descent. We show that SynthNet can learn to synthesize a wide variety of sounds, from simple sine waves to complex instrument timbres, by training on a small set of target audio samples. Our results demonstrate that SynthNet can effectively learn the parameters of a synthesizer to match a target sound, providing a new way to automate sound design and music synthesis.

However, in many real-world applications, exploration can be costly or dangerous, and the reward function may be difficult to specify. In this paper, we propose two methods for learning from human feedback: ReNeg and Backseat Driver. ReNeg uses a human to provide continuous feedback on the agent's actions, which is used to shape the reward function. Backseat Driver uses a human to provide continuous feedback on the agent's trajectory, which is used to guide the agent's exploration. We evaluate our methods on a set of toy problems and a more complex task, and show that they can significantly speed up learning and improve the final performance of the agent.

In this paper, we propose to utilize the concept of entanglement entropy to analyze the attention matrix in text matching tasks. By treating the attention matrix as a density matrix, we quantify the degree of correlation and information flow between the input sequences. We demonstrate that the entanglement entropy can effectively characterize the complexity of the attention distribution and reveal the transition from local to global feature aggregation across different layers of the model. Furthermore, we show that the entanglement entropy is positively correlated with the model's ability to capture semantic similarities, providing a theoretical lens to understand the attention mechanism's behavior. Our empirical results on several benchmark datasets validate that leveraging entanglement entropy not only enhances our understanding of the attention matrix but also provides a potential metric for optimizing the architecture of text matching models.

However, these algorithms typically rely on iterative pruning and retraining, which is computationally expensive. In this paper, we propose a new pruning method that is computationally efficient and provides a theoretical guarantee on the classification error. Our method uses a simple one-shot pruning strategy based on the magnitude of the weights, and we prove that the error introduced by pruning is bounded by a term that depends on the norm of the pruned weights. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and show that it achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art pruning methods while being significantly faster.

However, training a single adversary to remove sensitive information can be unstable and may not fully censor the representation. In this paper, we propose a new framework for censoring representations using multiple adversaries over random subspaces. Specifically, we project the learned representation into several random subspaces and train an adversary for each subspace. We show that this approach not only improves the stability of the training process but also leads to more effective censoring of the sensitive information. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its superiority over existing AFL methods.

However, these methods only capture the co-occurrence of two words, ignoring the higher-order interactions between words. In this paper, we propose a new approach to learn semantic word representations by factorizing a co-occurrence tensor. We show that our method can capture more complex semantic relationships than matrix factorization. We evaluate our approach on several word similarity and analogy tasks, and the results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

However, designing a reward function is often difficult and time-consuming. Imitation Learning (IL) is a promising alternative that allows an agent to learn from expert demonstrations. Behavioral Cloning (BC), the most common IL approach, suffers from the compounding error problem, where small mistakes lead the agent to states not seen in the training data. To address this, we propose SIMILE, a new IL framework that introduces sequential information into the learning process. By leveraging a sequence of past states and actions, SIMILE can better capture the temporal dependencies of the expert's behavior, leading to more robust and effective imitation. We evaluate SIMILE on several benchmark environments and demonstrate its superiority over existing IL methods.

While most attacks are input-specific, universal adversarial perturbations (UAPs) are input-agnostic and can fool a model on a large set of inputs. In this paper, we propose a new class of universal attacks that exploit the equivariance of the network. We show that for equivariant networks, a single perturbation can be transformed to create a set of perturbations that are effective across different transformations of the input. We evaluate our method on several equivariant architectures and datasets, demonstrating that our approach is more efficient and effective than existing UAP methods.

However, the high dimensionality and inherent noise of fMRI data make it challenging to model the underlying latent dynamics of neural activity. In this paper, we propose a generative framework based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to learn the distribution of brain activity and "hallucinate" synthetic fMRI patterns. We demonstrate that our model can capture the complex spatial and temporal correlations characteristic of human brain function and can be used to augment limited datasets for downstream tasks such as brain-state classification. Our results suggest that artificial neural networks can effectively approximate the generative processes of the human brain, providing a powerful tool for both data synthesis and the study of neural representations.

However, the mapping from the data space to the latent space is not explicitly learned during the training of GANs, which makes it difficult to find the latent vector that can reconstruct a given data point. In this paper, we propose a method to recycle the discriminator to improve the inference mapping of GANs. We use the discriminator as a feature extractor to map the data to a feature space, and then train a separate network to map these features to the latent space. Experimental results on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that our method can significantly improve the reconstruction quality compared to existing methods.

However, their utility for texture discrimination and novelty detection is less understood. In this paper, we compare the performance of a psychophysical model of texture representation with that of a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) for the task of novelty detection. We show that while the CNN achieves superior performance on standard classification tasks, the psychophysical model is more robust to changes in the statistics of the texture and generalizes better to unseen textures. We analyze the representations learned by the CNN and find that they are more specialized to the training set, whereas the psychophysical model captures more general properties of texture. Our results suggest that incorporating psychophysical priors into deep learning models could improve their generalization capabilities in texture analysis.

However, the standard DNNs are designed for Euclidean data and cannot be directly applied to manifold-valued data. In this paper, we propose ManifoldNet, a deep neural network architecture specifically designed for manifold-valued data. ManifoldNet incorporates the geometric structure of the manifold into the network layers by using Riemannian operations, such as the exponential and logarithmic maps. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ManifoldNet on several manifold-valued datasets, including the rotation group SO(3) and the sphere S2. Our results show that ManifoldNet outperforms existing methods in terms of both accuracy and convergence speed.

However, the standard approach of tuning these hyperparameters via a grid search or other black-box methods is computationally expensive and often impractical for large-scale models. In this paper, we propose a method for online hyperparameter adaptation that treats the hyperparameters as parameters to be optimized during the training process. We formulate this as a bilevel optimization problem and derive a proximal optimization algorithm that can be amortized over the training trajectory. Our approach allows for the dynamic adjustment of hyperparameters in a way that is computationally efficient and theoretically grounded. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several benchmark datasets, showing that it can achieve competitive or superior performance compared to manually tuned schedules and other online adaptation methods.

One such measure is the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), which leverages kernel methods to compare distributions in a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). However, the choice of the kernel is often data-dependent to maximize the power of the test, which leads to the problem of post-selection inference where the standard null distribution of the MMD statistic is no longer valid. To address this, we introduce the Incomplete Maximum Mean Discrepancy (IMMD) estimator, which enables valid statistical inference after the kernel has been selected. We derive the conditional distribution of the IMMD estimator and provide theoretical guarantees for the resulting p-values. Our empirical results on various datasets demonstrate that the proposed method effectively controls the Type I error while achieving superior power compared to traditional MMD tests with fixed kernels.

In this work, we investigate whether a two-stream convolutional neural network (CNN) can learn these features automatically from raw video data. We analyze the learned features of the spatial and temporal streams and compare them with the manually engineered features. Our results show that the two-stream CNN achieves comparable accuracy to the SVM and that the learned features are closely related to the manually engineered ones, providing insights into the representation learning process of the network.

Our approach leverages recurrent neural networks to capture the temporal dependencies in longitudinal data and employs a cause-specific hazard formulation to account for competing events. We evaluate our method on a large-scale dataset of primary care records, demonstrating that it significantly outperforms traditional survival models in terms of predictive accuracy. Our results indicate that the proposed deep learning approach can effectively model complex, high-dimensional patient trajectories to provide more precise and personalized risk predictions.

We provide a generalization bound for GANs and show that it is tighter than the bounds for other methods. Our results suggest that GANs are particularly effective for learning distributions with disconnected support.

However, the CRF layer is computationally expensive to train and evaluate, especially for large label sets. In this paper, we propose a new approach to sequence labeling based on actor-critic reinforcement learning. Our method replaces the CRF layer with an actor-critic framework, where the actor predicts the labels and the critic estimates the value of the current state. We show that our approach is more efficient than the CRF-based approach and achieves comparable or better performance on several sequence labeling tasks, including named entity recognition and part-of-speech tagging.

However, 3D meshes are generally irregular, making it difficult to apply CNNs directly. In this paper, we propose a Convolutional Mesh Autoencoder (CMAE) for learning a compact representation of 3D face meshes. We define a convolution operation on the mesh that is invariant to the vertex ordering and the mesh topology. We then use an encoder-decoder architecture to learn a low-dimensional latent space that captures the essential geometric properties of the face. Our experiments on a large-scale dataset of 3D face scans demonstrate that CMAE can effectively compress 3D face meshes while preserving high-frequency details, and the learned latent space can be used for tasks such as face reconstruction and interpolation.

We show that these flows can be used to represent a wide range of distributions over discrete states, and we provide an efficient algorithm for sampling from them. We apply our method to the problem of variational inference in discrete dynamical systems and show that it significantly improves the performance of VAEs in terms of both reconstruction accuracy and the quality of the learned latent representations.

In this paper, we propose a Tree2Tree learning framework to map a source tree to a target tree. We introduce a Tree-LSTM based encoder to represent the source tree and a Tree-LSTM based decoder to generate the target tree. To address the problem of long-term dependency in tree-to-tree mapping, we propose a memory unit to store the intermediate states of the encoder and decoder, which can be accessed by an attention mechanism. We evaluate our model on the English-to-Chinese semantic parsing task and the results show that our model outperforms the baseline models.

However, simply removing units can lead to a significant drop in performance. In this paper, we propose Mean Replacement Pruning (MRP), a new pruning method that replaces the pruned units with their mean values. We show that MRP can maintain the performance of the model while achieving the benefits of pruning. Our experiments on several datasets demonstrate that MRP outperforms existing pruning methods in terms of both accuracy and compression ratio.

However, most reinforcement learning (RL) agents rely on a form of semantic memory, where they learn a general policy that is averaged over many experiences. In this paper, we propose a method to incorporate episodic memory into RL agents, allowing them to remember and reuse specific past experiences to solve tasks more efficiently. We introduce an episodic memory module that stores transitions and retrieves them using a similarity-based mechanism. Our experiments on several benchmarks show that our approach significantly improves sample efficiency and performance, especially in environments with sparse rewards or long-term dependencies.

We then propose a generalized version of AGZ that can be applied to a wider range of problems, including those with continuous action spaces and partially observable states. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our generalized AGZ on several benchmark tasks, showing that it outperforms existing reinforcement learning methods.

We show that for a wide range of architectures and datasets, increasing the model size actually leads to faster convergence in terms of the number of iterations. We provide a theoretical analysis to explain this phenomenon, suggesting that overparameterization improves the condition number of the Hessian at the start of training. Our results suggest that overparameterization can be leveraged to speed up the training of deep neural networks.

We use a deep Q-network (DQN) to learn the optimal strategy for the game. Our experimental results show that our agent can outperform human players in a large number of games.

Specifically, SNOW enables a model to selectively "subscribe" to a subset of channels from a pre-trained knowledge base, integrating them with a small set of task-specific trainable parameters. By employing a channel pooling mechanism, the model can efficiently aggregate relevant features while minimizing redundant computations, thereby increasing training and serving throughput. This framework allows for rapid adaptation to new tasks without the need for full-model retraining, effectively addressing the challenge of catastrophic forgetting in lifelong learning. We evaluate SNOW on multiple benchmarks, demonstrating that it outperforms existing methods in both accuracy and efficiency for transfer and lifelong learning tasks.

However, they often suffer from catastrophic forgetting, where new knowledge overwrites previous knowledge. To address this, we propose a Dynamic Generative Memory (DGM) framework that learns a generative model to synthesize data from previous tasks. DGM uses a generative adversarial network (GAN) to approximate the distribution of the data seen so far, and uses the generated samples to replay previous knowledge while learning new tasks. We show that DGM effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting and outperforms existing methods on several benchmark datasets.

In this paper, we propose a novel few-shot learning framework that combines the power of Siamese networks and Support Vector Machines (SVM). Specifically, we use a Siamese network to learn a distance metric, which is then used as a kernel for an SVM classifier. Our approach allows the SVM to benefit from the representation learning capabilities of deep networks while maintaining the robust generalization properties of SVMs in low-data regimes. We evaluate our method on several few-shot learning benchmarks and demonstrate that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

We analyze the performance of the composite neural network from the perspective of function composition. We prove that the composite neural network can represent any function that can be represented by the individual neural networks. We also provide a theoretical analysis of the generalization error of the composite neural network. Finally, we conduct experiments to evaluate the performance of the composite neural network on several benchmark datasets, and the results demonstrate that the composite neural network can achieve better performance than the individual neural networks.

We propose a method that uses a memory buffer to store previously visited states and their associated rewards, and a recall mechanism to retrieve similar states to guide exploration. We show that our method significantly improves exploration efficiency in environments with sparse rewards, compared to standard exploration strategies like $\epsilon$-greedy or intrinsic motivation based on state novelty. Our results demonstrate that explicit recall of past experiences can be a powerful tool for overcoming the challenges of exploration in complex reinforcement learning tasks.

However, traditional anomaly detection methods often struggle to identify sophisticated adversarial examples designed to mimic normal data. In this paper, we propose a novel unsupervised framework for adversarial anomaly detection based on One-Class Support Vector Machines (OC-SVM). Our approach integrates an adversarial training mechanism that iteratively generates challenging anomalies to refine the decision boundary of the OC-SVM, thereby enhancing its ability to detect subtle deviations. We demonstrate through extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets that our method outperforms existing unsupervised anomaly detection techniques in terms of both detection accuracy and robustness against adversarial perturbations.

Specifically, we show that the best single model performance is a biased estimator of the architecture's performance and that this bias can be significant. We propose using the average performance of several models as a more reliable estimate and provide a method for determining the number of models needed to achieve a desired level of confidence. We apply our method to several common deep learning architectures and show that it can lead to different conclusions about their relative performance.

However, MAML assumes that the task distribution is unimodal, which may not hold in practice when tasks are grouped into distinct clusters. In such cases, a single initialization may be suboptimal for all tasks. We propose a framework that extends MAML to handle multimodal task distributions by learning a mixture of initializations. By incorporating a task-conditioned selection mechanism, our method can identify the most relevant meta-prior for a given task, thereby improving the efficiency and effectiveness of the adaptation process. We evaluate our approach on a variety of synthetic and real-world benchmarks, demonstrating that it consistently outperforms MAML, particularly as the multimodality of the task distribution increases.

Specifically, we propose a persona-based hredGAN (p-hredGAN) that incorporates persona information into the latent variable of the hredGAN to guide the generation of responses. To ensure that the generated responses are consistent with the persona and the dialogue context, we introduce a persona-based discriminator that distinguishes between the ground-truth response and the generated response given the persona and the context. We evaluate our model on the Persona-Chat dataset and the results show that our model outperforms the baseline models in terms of both automatic metrics and human evaluation.

In this paper, we propose a method to leverage weakly paired bilingual documents to improve NMT performance. We first use a sentence-level alignment method to extract parallel sentences from bilingual documents. Then, we use these extracted parallel sentences to pre-train the NMT model. Finally, we fine-tune the model on the small amount of gold parallel data. Our experiments on English-Chinese and English-French language pairs show that our method significantly improves the translation quality, especially for low-resource settings.

Specifically, the number of parameters in fully connected layers grows quadratically with the dimensionality of the hidden layers, often leading to overfitting and prohibitive computational costs. To address this, we introduce block diagonal inner product layers, which constrain the weight matrices to a block diagonal structure, thereby reducing the number of trainable parameters and the computational complexity of the forward and backward passes. We provide a theoretical justification for this architecture and evaluate its performance on a variety of tasks, including image classification and regression. Our experimental results show that block diagonal layers can achieve performance competitive with standard dense layers while significantly reducing the model size and improving training speed. We conclude that this structural constraint acts as an effective form of regularization, enhancing the generalization capabilities of the network.

Imitation learning (IL) can alleviate these challenges by leveraging expert demonstrations. However, adversarial IL methods often struggle with high-dimensional visual observations, as the discriminator can easily overfit to irrelevant image features, leading to training instability. In this paper, we propose a framework for visual imitation learning that utilizes a minimal adversary. By restricting the adversary to a low-dimensional latent representation, we prevent it from becoming too powerful relative to the policy, thereby stabilizing the adversarial training process. We demonstrate on several visual benchmarks that our minimal adversary significantly improves sample efficiency and performance compared to standard adversarial imitation learning.

However, the effect of low-precision training on the convergence of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is not well understood. In this paper, we study the convergence of SGD with low-precision gradients. We provide dimension-free convergence bounds for a class of low-precision quantization schemes, including the stochastic rounding. Our results show that the convergence rate of low-precision SGD is the same as that of full-precision SGD, provided that the precision is sufficiently high. We also provide a practical guideline for choosing the precision of gradients.

However, existing methods often struggle to efficiently manage and retrieve relevant information from extensive contexts. In this paper, we propose "Lift-the-flap," a novel framework that explicitly addresses the what, where, and when of context reasoning. Our approach employs a selective attention mechanism to identify salient information (what), a structured memory layout to organize this knowledge (where), and a dynamic triggering module to determine the optimal time for retrieval (when). We evaluate our method on several challenging benchmarks, demonstrating that Lift-the-flap significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both accuracy and efficiency.

In this paper, we propose a novel framework to perform deep neuroevolution in a low dimensional latent space. We first train an autoencoder to map the high dimensional parameter space of a neural network into a low dimensional latent space. Then, we perform neuroevolution in this latent space to find the optimal parameters. Our experiments on several Atari games show that our method can achieve competitive performance with significantly fewer samples and search steps compared to state-of-the-art deep neuroevolution methods.

In this paper, we propose the Non-Synergistic Variational Autoencoder (NS-VAE), which aims to minimize the synergistic information between the latent variables to encourage disentanglement. We introduce a new regularization term based on the concept of synergistic information to penalize the dependencies between the latent factors. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that NS-VAE can learn more disentangled representations than $\beta$-VAE and FactorVAE, while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality.

We use a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) to learn the latent topic distribution of the conversation and use the sampled topic to guide the response generation. Experimental results on the DailyDialog dataset show that our model outperforms the baseline seq2seq model in terms of both diversity and quality of the generated responses.

However, standard convolution is typically defined on Euclidean grids, which may not be suitable for data with non-Euclidean structures or inherent hierarchies. In this paper, we propose Volumetric Convolution, a novel operation designed for automatic representation learning within the unit ball. By leveraging the geometric properties of hyperbolic space, our method can more effectively capture the hierarchical nature of complex data. We provide a theoretical framework for this operation and demonstrate its superiority over standard convolutional neural networks through extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets, showing significant improvements in both representation accuracy and computational efficiency.

By structuring the learning process hierarchically, the agent can decompose complex goals into a sequence of simpler sub-goals defined in the latent space, thereby significantly reducing the exploration search space. We evaluate our method on several challenging multitask benchmarks, demonstrating that it improves sample efficiency and final performance compared to state-of-the-art hierarchical RL algorithms.

In this paper, we show that the standard momentum schemes can fail to converge to the optimal solution in the presence of noise, and we propose a new momentum scheme that is robust to noise and provides a faster convergence rate than SGD. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed method and demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments on several benchmark datasets.

However, the computational cost of calculating and inverting the Hessian matrix is often prohibitive. In this paper, we propose a block-diagonal approximation to the Hessian matrix, which significantly reduces the computational overhead while maintaining the benefits of second-order optimization. We show that our method converges faster than first-order methods and is more computationally efficient than full Hessian-free optimization. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in training deep neural networks.

Unlike existing methods that require labeled data for each attribute, VarNet learns to disentangle the attributes in an unsupervised manner. We propose a novel architecture that consists of an encoder, a variation network, and a decoder. The encoder maps the input to a latent space, the variation network learns to shift the latent representation along specific attribute directions, and the decoder reconstructs the manipulated input. We demonstrate the effectiveness of VarNet on several image datasets, showing that it can successfully manipulate attributes such as pose, expression, and lighting without any supervision.

However, the large number of parameters in RNNs can lead to overfitting and high computational costs. In this paper, we propose Generalized Tensor Models (GTMs) for RNNs, which use tensor decompositions to reduce the number of parameters while maintaining the expressive power of the network. We show that GTMs can be used to implement various types of RNNs, including LSTMs and GRUs, and that they can significantly reduce the number of parameters without sacrificing performance. We evaluate our proposed GTMs on several benchmark datasets and show that they outperform standard RNNs in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

However, these methods typically rely on a single scalar reward function, which often fails to capture the multifaceted and sometimes conflicting motivations that drive human behavior. In this paper, we propose Vector-valued Inverse Reinforcement Learning (V-IRL), a framework that models human behavior as the optimization of multiple, distinct reward functions. By representing rewards as vectors, V-IRL can disentangle competing objectives and provide a more nuanced understanding of the trade-offs humans make during decision-making. We evaluate our approach on human gameplay data, demonstrating that V-IRL significantly improves the accuracy of behavior prediction and provides interpretable insights into human motivations. Our results suggest that moving beyond scalar rewards is essential for modeling the complexity of human-like agency.

This distance, which we call the holographic distance, is based on the idea of representing a point set as a single point in a higher-dimensional space. We show that the holographic distance is a metric and that it is computationally efficient to compute. We also introduce several other point set distances and compare them with the holographic distance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the holographic distance in several machine learning tasks, including point set registration and point set classification.

However, the quality of the resulting approximation is often limited by the choice of the variational family. In this paper, we propose a method to refine the variational posterior by iteratively optimizing a set of parameters that define a transformation of the initial variational distribution. We show that our method can be viewed as a way to iteratively improve the approximation of the posterior distribution by moving towards the true posterior in the space of distributions. We evaluate our method on several synthetic and real-world datasets and show that it consistently improves the quality of the variational posterior compared to standard VI methods.

One promising solution is Homomorphic Encryption (HE), which enables computations to be performed directly on encrypted data. However, the computational overhead of Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) remains prohibitively high, particularly for the non-linear activation functions common in deep neural networks. To address these challenges, we propose a hybrid homomorphic encryption framework that leverages the efficiency of partially homomorphic encryption for linear layers and a secure multi-party computation protocol for non-linearities. Our method significantly reduces the latency of encrypted inference while maintaining the precision of the original model. We evaluate our approach on several standard image classification tasks, demonstrating that our scheme achieves a favorable trade-off between computational efficiency and privacy preservation.

In this paper, we propose a framework for constructing deep Lipschitz networks that maintain a controlled Lipschitz constant across multiple layers to stabilize the training of GANs. We introduce Dudley GANs, which leverage the Dudley entropy integral to provide theoretical bounds on the generalization error of the discriminator. By bounding the covering numbers of the discriminator's function class, we show that our approach prevents the discriminator from overfitting to the generator's current distribution, thereby mitigating the vanishing gradient problem. Our experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method leads to more stable training and superior sample quality compared to existing Lipschitz-constrained GAN architectures.

However, most existing meta-learning methods share a common feature space across all tasks, which may not be optimal for each individual task. In this paper, we propose a novel meta-learning framework that learns an individualized feature space for each task. Specifically, we introduce a task-specific feature transformation module that adapts the global feature space to a task-specific one. Our experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art meta-learning methods.

While symbolic reasoners are sound and complete, they struggle with the noise and uncertainty of natural language. Conversely, neural models are robust to noise but often lack the transparency and rigor of symbolic logic. In this paper, we propose a scalable neural theorem prover that combines the strengths of both approaches. Our model uses a neural network to learn a set of rules for reasoning over a KB and text, and then applies these rules in a symbolic fashion to derive answers. We evaluate our approach on several benchmarks and show that it outperforms existing baselines in terms of accuracy and scalability.

However, most existing methods focus on designing a static architecture that is shared across all inputs, which may lead to redundant computations for simple instances. In this paper, we propose Instance-aware Selective Branching Networks (ISBNet), a novel dynamic architecture that can adaptively select the most suitable computation path for each instance. Specifically, we introduce a lightweight gating module to decide whether to execute a branch or skip it, thereby reducing the overall computational cost while maintaining high accuracy. We further propose a joint optimization strategy to train the gating module and the main network simultaneously. Extensive experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that ISBNet can significantly reduce the average FLOPs and latency compared to state-of-the-art static and dynamic networks, achieving a better trade-off between efficiency and performance.

However, in the real world, an agent is often required to perform a variety of tasks in a variety of environments. In this paper, we propose a universal agent that can disentangle the environment from the task. Our agent learns a representation of the environment and a representation of the task, and then uses these representations to perform the task in the environment. We evaluate our agent on a set of synthetic environments and tasks, and show that it can generalize to unseen environments and tasks.

However, in many real-world scenarios, coordination is expensive, and agents cannot afford to communicate or synchronize their actions at every time step. In this paper, we propose an event-based deep RL framework to learn when to coordinate. Specifically, we introduce a triggering mechanism that allows agents to communicate only when necessary, thereby reducing the communication overhead while maintaining high performance. We evaluate our method on several challenging MARL benchmarks and demonstrate that it significantly outperforms existing baselines in terms of both efficiency and effectiveness.

In this work, we analyze the relationship between model accuracy and policy performance, demonstrating that the bias introduced by the learned model can create a performance ceiling that cannot be overcome by simply increasing the amount of training data. We propose a theoretical framework to quantify this bias and introduce a method to mitigate its effects by integrating model-free updates. Our experiments across several benchmark environments show that our approach maintains the sample efficiency of model-based methods while matching the asymptotic performance of model-free baselines.

In this paper, we investigate whether this principle can be used to train deep neural networks in a layer-by-layer fashion. We propose a layer-by-layer training method based on the IB principle, where each layer is trained to maximize its MI with the target labels while minimizing its MI with the input of the previous layer. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and show that it can achieve competitive performance compared to standard end-to-end training, while significantly reducing the training time and avoiding the vanishing gradient problem. Furthermore, we provide an analysis of the MI between the layers and the target labels, showing that our method effectively implements the IB principle.

To address this challenge, we propose a novel model compression framework based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Our approach leverages an adversarial training objective to distill the knowledge of a large teacher model into a compact student model, where a discriminator is trained to distinguish between the predictions of the teacher and the student. By framing the compression process as a minimax game, the student model is encouraged to mimic the teacher's output distribution more effectively than with traditional distillation losses. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate that it achieves a superior trade-off between model size and accuracy compared to state-of-the-art pruning and quantization techniques.

However, most of these methods assume that the demonstrator has a single intention for a given state, which is often not the case in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we propose a new framework for imitation learning that can handle multiple intentions by incorporating a latent variable to represent the intention of the demonstrator. We show that our method can effectively learn multiple skills from a single dataset of demonstrations and can generalize to new goals. We evaluate our approach on a robotic manipulation task and demonstrate its effectiveness compared to baseline methods.

However, they often struggle with generalization when the training data is limited. To address this, we propose MixFeat, a novel regularization method that mixes features in the latent space to learn a more discriminative representation. Unlike traditional mixup techniques that operate on the input space, MixFeat interpolates hidden representations, forcing the network to learn a more structured and separable latent space. This approach encourages the model to maintain linear transitions between classes, effectively smoothing the decision boundaries. Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that MixFeat significantly improves generalization performance and robustness over existing data augmentation methods.

However, existing methods mostly rely on a large number of seed alignments, which are expensive to obtain. In this paper, we propose a weakly-supervised knowledge graph alignment framework based on adversarial learning. Specifically, we first employ a graph convolutional network to learn the embeddings of entities and relations. Then, we use a generative adversarial network to align the embeddings of entities and relations from two knowledge graphs. To further improve the alignment performance, we introduce a cycle-consistency loss to ensure the mapping is bijective. Experimental results on two real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

In this paper, we propose a simple approach to this problem by introducing a new loss function, called the Gambler's Loss. The Gambler's Loss is designed to be robust to label noise by limiting the influence of samples that are likely to be mislabeled, effectively treating the training process as a risk-managed bet on label correctness. We show that the Gambler's Loss is a generalization of several existing robust loss functions and that it can be easily implemented. Our experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that the Gambler's Loss outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and robustness to noise.

Specifically, it leverages data parallelism, model parallelism, and a newly proposed hidden-dimension parallelism. By partitioning the hidden dimensions of tensors across multiple devices, DeePa can effectively utilize the available memory and computational resources, reducing the communication overhead and improving the overall training efficiency. We evaluate DeePa on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate that it achieves significant speedups compared to existing frameworks, while maintaining the same model accuracy.

However, these models often struggle to provide reliable uncertainty estimates, frequently resulting in overconfident predictions. In this paper, we introduce Learning with Reflective Likelihoods, a novel framework that iteratively refines the likelihood function by reflecting the model's predictive uncertainty back into the training objective. This mechanism allows the model to better account for epistemic uncertainty and improve its calibration. We provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed method and demonstrate its effectiveness on several benchmark datasets, showing that Reflective Likelihoods significantly improve model robustness and generalization compared to standard maximum likelihood estimation.

In this work, we extend this framework to the domain of musical audio. We propose a method that leverages multiple time-frequency representations to capture the diverse characteristics of musical style and content. Specifically, we utilize the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) and the Constant-Q Transform (CQT) to represent the audio signals, enabling the model to capture both the fine-grained spectral details and the harmonic structure of the music. We employ a pre-trained VGG-19 network to extract features from these representations and optimize a new audio signal that combines the content of a source clip with the style of a target clip. Our results demonstrate that using multiple representations allows for a more effective transfer of musical style, capturing both rhythmic and timbral qualities more accurately than methods relying on a single representation.

To reduce the computation, Winograd convolution is widely used to accelerate the convolution operation. However, the Winograd convolution is not compatible with the weight pruning, as the pruning of a single weight in the spatial domain will lead to a dense weight in the Winograd domain. In this paper, we propose a novel Spatial-Winograd Pruning (SWP) method to enable sparse Winograd convolution. Specifically, we prune the weights in the spatial domain such that the corresponding Winograd weights are also sparse. We show that by pruning a specific group of weights in the spatial domain, we can obtain a sparse Winograd weight. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and show that SWP can significantly reduce the computation and memory requirements of Winograd convolution while maintaining the accuracy of the CNNs.

However, inducing sparsity in these representations often requires restrictive priors that can limit the model's ability to capture complex dependencies. In this paper, we propose the Deep Copula Information Bottleneck (DCIB), a framework that integrates the Information Bottleneck principle with copula-based modeling of the latent space. By leveraging copulas to decouple the marginal distributions of the latent variables from their joint dependence structure, DCIB enables the use of sparsity-promoting priors while maintaining a flexible representation of the underlying data manifold. We demonstrate through experiments on several benchmark datasets that DCIB learns more interpretable and sparse latent representations than existing variational information bottleneck methods. Our results indicate that the proposed approach effectively balances compression and predictive power, leading to improved performance on downstream tasks.

However, most of these models are designed for a specific task or a small set of tasks, and they often struggle to generalize to new tasks. In this paper, we propose MEMO, a deep network that can flexibly combine episodic memories to solve a wide range of reasoning tasks. MEMO uses a memory-augmented neural network that can store and retrieve information from a large number of episodic memories. We show that MEMO can solve all the bAbI tasks and can also generalize to new tasks without further training. Our results demonstrate that the ability to flexibly combine episodic memories is crucial for solving complex reasoning tasks.

To reduce the computational cost, network pruning has been widely used to remove redundant parameters. However, most existing pruning methods rely on manual design of pruning heuristics or require expensive search processes to find the optimal pruning ratio for each layer. In this paper, we propose a novel layer-wise pruning method to automatically search for an efficient DenseNet. Specifically, we formulate the pruning ratio search as a reinforcement learning problem, where an agent learns to determine the pruning ratio for each layer to maximize the model's performance while satisfying a given resource constraint. Experimental results on ImageNet demonstrate that our method can significantly reduce the number of parameters and FLOPs of DenseNet while maintaining competitive accuracy.

However, we argue that this approach is suboptimal because it does not explicitly encourage the model to learn a representation that is robust to task transitions. In this paper, we propose a new method that leverages a multi-task teacher to guide the student model in learning a more generalizable representation. By distilling knowledge from a teacher trained on multiple tasks, the student can better maintain performance on previous tasks while learning new ones. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and show that it significantly outperforms existing methods in mitigating catastrophic forgetting.

However, existing probabilistic embeddings are typically limited to representing symmetric relations (e.g., similarity) and struggle to capture asymmetric relations (e.g., hyponymy). In this paper, we propose Density Order Embeddings (DOE), a new framework for representing asymmetric relations using probability densities. We show that by using a specific family of distributions, we can represent the asymmetric relation of 'is-a' as a containment relation between densities. We evaluate our model on several word hierarchy datasets and show that it outperforms existing baselines in capturing asymmetric relations while maintaining the benefits of probabilistic embeddings.

However, the computational cost of the softmax layer is often the bottleneck during inference, especially when the vocabulary size is large. To address this, we propose a learning-to-screen approach that efficiently filters out a large number of unlikely candidates before the final softmax computation. We introduce a lightweight screening network that predicts whether a word is likely to be in the top-k candidates. By training this screening network together with the main model, we can significantly reduce the number of dot products required for inference without sacrificing much accuracy. Our experiments on several large-scale datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a substantial speedup in inference time while maintaining competitive performance.

MÊLÉE learns a policy that can be quickly adapted to a new bandit task by observing a small number of interactions. We show that MÊLÉE can be implemented as a recurrent neural network that takes the history of interactions as input and outputs the action probabilities. We evaluate MÊLÉE on a variety of synthetic and real-world bandit tasks and show that it outperforms standard exploration strategies such as $\epsilon$-greedy and Upper Confidence Bound (UCB).

Our approach is based on a differentiable implementation of Sparse Distributed Memory (SDM), enabling the system to be optimized via backpropagation. By mapping inputs to a high-dimensional space through random projections, the Kanerva Machine stores patterns in a distributed fashion, which facilitates rapid adaptation to new data. We show that by sampling from this distributed representation, the model can generate novel samples that resemble the training data. Experimental results on several benchmarks demonstrate that the Kanerva Machine achieves a superior balance between memory efficiency and generative performance compared to existing associative memory models.

However, the geometric properties of the resulting binary weights are not well understood. In this paper, we analyze the distribution of binary weights in high-dimensional space and show that they tend to be concentrated on the surface of a hypersphere. We further show that this concentration is a result of the interaction between the latent weights and the binary quantization process. Our results provide a theoretical understanding of why binary neural networks can be trained effectively and suggest new ways to improve their performance.

While the score function estimator is general, it often suffers from high variance. The reparameterization trick can significantly reduce variance, but it requires the distribution $q_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}$ to be reparameterizable. In this paper, we propose a general framework for gradient estimation, which we call the GO gradient. The GO gradient generalizes both the score function estimator and the reparameterization trick, and can be used to derive new, low-variance gradient estimators for a wide class of distributions. We provide a theoretical analysis of the GO gradient and show that it can be used to improve the performance of various machine learning algorithms, including variational autoencoders and reinforcement learning.

To address this, we propose a framework to train implicit generative models by using an explicit model as a teacher. The explicit model is trained to approximate the distribution of the implicit model, and the implicit model is then updated to minimize the divergence between the explicit model and the target data distribution. We show that this approach leads to more stable training and better sample quality compared to existing methods. Our experiments on several datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

However, for many models, the likelihood is intractable, and we must rely on approximations. In this paper, we propose a general framework for training generative latent models by minimizing a variational upper bound on any f-divergence. We show that our framework generalizes the variational autoencoder (VAE) and the adversarial autoencoder (AAE), and we provide a method for optimizing the bound using a combination of stochastic gradient descent and a discriminator network. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets and show that it can lead to better sample quality and more robust latent representations than the VAE.

However, the requirement that the variational posterior must have a tractable density often limits the expressiveness of the approximate posterior. In this paper, we propose Kernel Implicit Variational Inference (KIVI), a new framework for variational inference that allows for highly flexible variational posteriors without requiring a tractable density. KIVI leverages the power of kernel methods to represent the variational posterior as a mixture of kernels, which can be efficiently sampled from and optimized. We show that KIVI can effectively capture complex posterior distributions and outperforms existing variational inference methods on several synthetic and real-world datasets.

A common way to achieve this is by using Successor Features (SF), which decouple the environment dynamics from the reward function. However, SFs are typically tied to a specific state-action space, limiting their applicability to tasks with different spaces. In this paper, we propose Universal Successor Features (USF), which generalize SFs by introducing a universal representation space. This allows the agent to transfer knowledge across tasks with different state and action spaces by learning a mapping from the task-specific spaces to the universal space. We provide theoretical guarantees for the convergence of USF and demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments on a variety of transfer RL benchmarks, showing that USF significantly reduces the number of samples needed to learn a new task.

In this paper, we propose a flexible framework for the automated generation of recurrent neural network (RNN) architectures. We employ a reinforcement learning agent to explore a vast search space of possible cell configurations, including various gating mechanisms and connection patterns. By optimizing the architecture for a specific task, our method can discover novel RNN cells that outperform standard LSTMs and GRUs. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark datasets, demonstrating that the generated architectures achieve state-of-the-art performance while significantly reducing the need for manual design. Our results indicate that automated search can effectively uncover efficient and high-performing architectures tailored to specific sequence-modeling challenges.

However, its theoretical foundation remains unclear. In this paper, we provide a theoretical interpretation of RAML by showing that it is equivalent to estimating the softmax Q-distribution. We prove that the RAML objective is a lower bound on the log-likelihood of the softmax Q-distribution. Furthermore, we show that the RAML objective is a special case of the maximum likelihood estimation for the softmax Q-distribution when the reward is a binary indicator. Our theoretical analysis provides a new perspective on why RAML works and suggests a way to improve it by incorporating more general reward functions.

Specifically, we first establish the convergence of the empirical risk, its gradient and its stationary points to their population counterparts as the number of training samples increases. Then, we analyze the convergence rates of these quantities and show that the convergence performance is determined by the network width and the number of training samples. Finally, we provide a theoretical analysis of the generalization error of DNNs and show that the generalization error is bounded by the difference between the empirical risk and the population risk. Our results provide a theoretical foundation for understanding the training and generalization of DNNs.

In this paper, we propose to view the generative process as an inverse problem. We use the scattering transform, a deep network with fixed weights, to provide a stable and translation-invariant representation of the images. We show that the generative network can be interpreted as an approximate inverse of the scattering transform. We provide a theoretical framework for this interpretation and demonstrate its effectiveness on several image datasets.

However, most existing models are black-boxes and lack interpretability. In this paper, we propose a novel framework to learn corresponded rationales for text matching, which identifies the most relevant snippets from both texts that support the prediction. Our approach employs a dual-attention mechanism to extract these rationales and a consistency constraint to ensure that the selected snippets are mutually supportive. We evaluate our method on the SNLI and SQuAD datasets, and the results show that our model not only maintains competitive performance but also provides human-interpretable rationales that align well with human intuition.

However, the evaluation of GANs remains a challenging problem, as there is no single metric that can capture all aspects of the generated distribution. In this paper, we propose to evaluate GANs using the same divergences that are used for their training. We show that these divergences can provide a quantitative measure of the quality of the generated samples and the diversity of the generated distribution. We evaluate our proposed method on several benchmark datasets and show that it correlates well with human judgment and other existing evaluation metrics.

The acRNN is trained to predict the next frame of a motion sequence given its own previous predictions, rather than the ground truth. This approach allows the network to learn to compensate for the accumulation of errors that typically occurs during the generation of long sequences, a problem known as drift. We evaluate our method on a large dataset of human motion capture and show that it can generate realistic, diverse, and temporally consistent motions over extended periods. Our results demonstrate that acRNN significantly outperforms standard RNNs and other baseline methods in terms of both visual quality and stability.

However, most existing DNA classification methods rely on one-dimensional sequence representations, which often ignore the spatial information provided by the chromatin structure. In this work, we propose a novel framework that transforms DNA sequences into a two-dimensional image representation, allowing the model to capture structural patterns and long-range dependencies. We then employ a convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify these images, leveraging the ability of CNNs to extract hierarchical spatial features. Our results demonstrate that this image-based approach outperforms traditional sequence-based models, providing a more effective way to analyze the functional properties of DNA through its structural representation.

We propose that the semantic mapping is the one that minimizes a specific complexity measure, based on the intuition that the simplest transformation is the most likely to preserve semantic structure. We provide a theoretical analysis of the conditions under which this minimal complexity criterion identifies the correct mapping and evaluate our approach on several unsupervised domain translation tasks. Our results show that incorporating a complexity prior allows for the discovery of robust semantic mappings without any paired training data.

However, the training of these learned optimizers typically requires the gradients of the objective function, which may be unavailable or computationally expensive to compute in some applications. In this paper, we propose a novel framework to learn the update rules of optimization algorithms using only a zeroth-order oracle, i.e., the function values of the objective. We show that the zeroth-order gradient estimator can be used to update the parameters of the learned optimizer. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of the convergence of our proposed method. Experimental results on several benchmark problems demonstrate that our zeroth-order L2L approach can effectively learn optimization algorithms that perform competitively with those trained with first-order information.

In this paper, we propose a new method to stabilize TD learning by constraining the gradients of the value function. We show that our method converges to the TD fixed point and provide a theoretical analysis of its convergence rate. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several benchmark tasks.

However, the computational cost of applying these transformations to all training examples can be prohibitive. In this paper, we propose a method to efficiently perform data augmentation by subsampling the training set. We show that by carefully selecting a subset of the data to augment, we can achieve similar performance to full augmentation while significantly reducing the training time. Our experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach is effective and efficient.

However, the mechanism by which the brain achieves rotation invariance—the ability to recognize an object regardless of its orientation—remains poorly understood. In this paper, we propose a rotation-invariant clustering method to analyze the population responses of V1 neurons. By leveraging the group-theoretic properties of rotations, our method identifies clusters of neurons that respond consistently to rotated versions of the same stimulus. We demonstrate that our approach can effectively group neurons with similar orientation preferences and uncover rotationally invariant patterns of activity. Our results suggest that the V1 population encodes visual information in a way that is robust to rotations, providing a biological precedent for the use of group-equivariant architectures in deep learning.

To learn the representation of graphs, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been proposed. However, most GNNs focus on node-level representations and struggle to capture the global structure of graphs. To address this, graph pooling is introduced to learn hierarchical representations of graphs. Existing graph pooling methods often rely on a single pooling strategy, which may not be sufficient to capture the diverse structural patterns in graphs. In this paper, we propose MxPool, a multiplex pooling framework for hierarchical graph representation learning. MxPool employs multiple pooling strategies in parallel to capture different structural properties of graphs and then aggregates the results. We evaluate MxPool on several graph classification benchmarks and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving the performance of GNNs.

However, these methods typically treat all misclassifications as equally costly, which is often not the case in real-world applications. In this paper, we propose a cost-sensitive framework for certified robustness, where different misclassifications are assigned different costs. We introduce a new training objective and a certification method that provide guarantees on the cost-weighted error rate under adversarial perturbations. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate that it can significantly improve the performance of classifiers in scenarios where certain misclassifications are more critical than others.

We prove that the recovered sparse principal components are close to the true sparse principal components with high probability. We also provide a computationally efficient algorithm to implement our approach and demonstrate its effectiveness through numerical experiments.

While standard variational autoencoders (VAEs) assume a factorized prior, we introduce a structured prior that allows the model to capture dependencies between latent variables. We use a continuous relaxation of the structure to enable joint optimization of the structure and the model parameters. Our experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that our method can recover the true latent structure and improve the generative performance of VAEs.

In the context of graphs, node embeddings have emerged as a powerful tool for a wide range of tasks, such as link prediction and node classification. However, most existing methods for learning node embeddings are computationally expensive, especially when dealing with large-scale graphs. In this paper, we propose a new approach for learning node embeddings based on ego-centric representations. Our method, which we call Fast Node Embeddings (FNE), leverages the local structure of the graph to learn representations that are both efficient to compute and effective for downstream tasks. We show that FNE can significantly reduce the training time compared to state-of-the-art methods while maintaining competitive performance. We evaluate our approach on several real-world datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness and scalability.

While stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants are the standard tools for this task, they often suffer from slow convergence and a high sensitivity to hyperparameter selection. In this paper, we propose Deep Frank-Wolfe (DFW), an optimization framework that adapts the projection-free Frank-Wolfe algorithm to the non-convex and unconstrained setting of deep neural networks. By introducing a dynamic constraint set, DFW avoids the computationally expensive projection steps typically associated with constrained optimization while maintaining the efficiency of linear oracles. We provide a theoretical analysis of the convergence properties of DFW and demonstrate its effectiveness on several benchmark datasets, showing that it can outperform SGD in terms of both convergence speed and robustness.

In this paper, we propose a new unsupervised learning algorithm for the extraction of visual features, based on the principle of homeostatic plasticity. The algorithm is designed to maintain the activity of the neurons within a target range, and it has been shown to learn a set of features that are similar to those found in the primary visual cortex. We evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm on a set of natural images and show that it is capable of learning a diverse set of features, including edges and Gabor-like filters, without the need for any labeled data.

In this paper, we propose a new parameterization of the weight matrices based on the singular value decomposition (SVD) to stabilize the gradients. Specifically, we decompose the weight matrix into two orthogonal matrices and a diagonal matrix of singular values. By constraining the singular values to be close to one, we can prevent the gradients from vanishing or exploding. We show that our method is computationally efficient and can be easily integrated into existing deep learning frameworks. Experimental results on several benchmarks demonstrate that our method improves the training stability and performance of deep neural networks, particularly for RNNs.

However, the challenge lies in how to effectively identify the clean samples, as the labels are corrupted. In this paper, we propose a novel sample-selection framework based on the memorization effect, which suggests that deep neural networks tend to learn simple patterns first and memorize noisy labels later. Specifically, we formulate the sample-selection process as a search problem to find a subset of training samples that maximizes the model's performance on a small clean validation set. To solve this search problem efficiently, we employ a reinforcement learning-based approach. Extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art sample-selection methods in terms of classification accuracy.
